data.howToName: How to boil eggs from a cold start

description: Cold-start eggs go into cold water, come to a boil, then stand covered off the heat: 12 minutes for a large egg. Method and stand times by size.

examples.result: Four medium eggs, cold start: 9 minute stand.
steps: Put the eggs in a single layer and cover with cold water an inch over them.
Bring the water just to a boil over medium-high heat.
Take the pan off the heat, cover it, and let the eggs stand 9 minutes (American Egg Board, medium eggs).
Move the eggs to ice water for 10 minutes.

steps: Put the eggs in a single layer and cover with cold water an inch over them.
Bring the water just to a boil over medium-high heat.
Take the pan off the heat, cover it, and let the eggs stand 15 minutes (American Egg Board, extra-large eggs).
Move the eggs to ice water for 10 minutes.

faqs.answer: The total is longer, the hands-on time is shorter. A large egg stands 12 minutes off the heat after the water boils, against 10 minutes 10 seconds at a full boil by the formula, plus the minutes the water takes to come to the boil. You do nothing during the stand, which is the point of the method.
faqs.question: Does a cold start take longer?

faqs.answer: There is no thermal shock. The egg warms with the water, so the shell heats evenly and the air pocket expands gently. Eggs lowered into boiling water crack far more often, especially straight from the fridge.
faqs.question: Why do cold-start eggs crack less?

faqs.answer: Not recommended. A soft or jammy yolk needs precise timing, and the cold start's timing depends on how fast your stove heats the pot. For soft and jammy eggs, boil the water first and use the timer.
faqs.question: Can I cold-start soft eggs?

faqs.answer: Use a lid, less water, and the biggest burner. The stand time stays the same once the water boils: 12 minutes for a large egg. The come-to-boil time is the only part that changes, and it is dead time either way.
faqs.question: What if the water takes forever to boil?

faqs.answer: Colorado State University Extension simmers the eggs for 5 minutes first above 5,000 feet, then lets them stand 15 minutes for large eggs or 20 for extra-large. Use that method rather than the sea-level stand times if you live high up.
faqs.question: How does a cold start work at altitude?

felicityNote: Cold start is my method for a big batch of hard-boiled eggs. No cracks, no watching the pot, and the timer only starts when the water boils.

parts.meaning: The constant from the egg's thermal properties: density 1.038 g per cubic cm, specific heat 3.7, thermal conductivity 0.0054.
The weight of the egg in grams. A large egg is 57 g (USDA size).
The starting temperature of the egg: 4°C from the fridge, 20°C at room temperature.
The boiling point of the water: 100°C at sea level, lower at altitude.
The target temperature at the edge of the yolk: 84°C for hard-boiled.
The American Egg Board stand for a large egg, covered off the heat after the water boils. The formula does not compute this; it is the Board's tested time.

formula.text: The Williams formula assumes water already at the boil, so for a cold start it gives the boiling-phase time only. For a large fridge egg at sea level, hard-boiled: 27 × 57^(2/3) × ln(0.76 × (4 - 100) / (84 - 100)) = 608 seconds, about 10 minutes 10 seconds. The cold-start total adds the come-to-boil time, and the American Egg Board stand of 12 minutes covers the cooking in the cooling water instead.

howToSteps.name: Eggs in cold water
howToSteps.text: Put the eggs in a single layer in a saucepan and cover with cold water an inch over them.

howToSteps.name: Bring to a boil
howToSteps.text: Heat over medium-high heat until the water just reaches a boil. Do not start the timer yet.

howToSteps.name: Off the heat, covered
howToSteps.text: Take the pan off the heat, put the lid on, and let the eggs stand: 12 minutes for large eggs, 9 for medium, 15 for extra-large.

howToSteps.name: Ice bath
howToSteps.text: Move the eggs to ice water for 10 minutes. This stops the cooking and makes peeling easier.

howToSteps.name: Peel
howToSteps.text: Tap both ends on the counter, roll gently, and peel under cold running water.

lede: Cold-start eggs go into cold water, come to the boil together, then stand covered off the heat: 12 minutes for a large egg, 9 for a medium, 15 for an extra-large. The Williams formula does not cover this method directly, because the water is warming the whole time.

title: How Long to Boil Eggs: Cold Start
tutorial: The cold start is the gentle way to boil eggs: eggs in a single layer, cold water an inch over them, heat on, and the eggs warm with the water. There is no thermal shock, so the shells almost never crack. The American Egg Board's version brings the water just to a boil, takes the pan off the heat, covers it, and lets the eggs stand: 12 minutes for a large egg, 9 for a medium, 15 for an extra-large.

The Williams formula does not describe this method, and it would be dishonest to pretend it does. The formula assumes the egg goes into water that is already boiling at a steady temperature. In a cold start the water warms from cold, the egg cooks during the whole climb, and how fast your stove heats the pot changes the result. No published model covers a cold start, so the stand times above come from the American Egg Board's tested method, not from the formula.

The calculator on this page still helps: it gives the boiling-phase time, the minutes the egg would need at a full boil. For a large fridge egg, hard-boiled, that is 10 minutes 10 seconds. Your cold-start total is that time plus the minutes the water takes to come to the boil, minus a little, because the egg cooks during the climb. The stand method sidesteps all of that by letting the eggs finish in the cooling water off the heat.

The cold start is best for hard-boiled eggs, where a minute either way does not matter much. It is a poor way to time a soft or jammy yolk, because the come-to-boil time varies with the stove and the pot, and a soft yolk forgives nothing. For soft and jammy eggs, boil the water first and use the timer.

At altitude the cold start needs more time, not less. Colorado State University Extension simmers the eggs for 5 minutes first above 5,000 feet, then lets them stand 15 minutes for large eggs or 20 for extra-large. If you live high up, use that method rather than the sea-level stand times.
